questions.q: Besides Guatemala, which country borders Mexico to the southeast?
questions.exp: Mexico is bordered by the United States to the north and by Guatemala and Belize to the southeast, and the Court places it firmly in North America. Its wine country lies far from that southern border: Baja California beside the United States line, and the high plateau of Coahuila and Querétaro in the north and centre.

questions.q: Which climate range does the Court give Mexico's wine regions?
questions.exp: Baja California's valleys are Mediterranean, dry in summer with slight winter rain and made workable by the cold Pacific, and the inland plateau shades into semi-desert, as at Parras in Coahuila. Baja lies at about thirty-two degrees north, the latitude of North Africa, so heat, not cold, is the problem Mexican vineyards solve.

questions.q: The Court describes valleys cutting through Baja's mountains to bring in Pacific fog and breezes. In which direction do they run?
questions.exp: Valleys running from the southwest towards the northeast open the Valle de Guadalupe region to the Pacific off Ensenada, so fog and sea air reach the vines each evening and pull the night temperature down. The Court's Certified profile of the valley adds its Mediterranean climate, its dominant share of Mexican wine and its standing as a modern winemaking and tourist destination.

questions.q: Away from the Pacific, what does the Court say gives Mexican vineyards cooler temperatures and cool nights?
questions.exp: In the mountains it is cooler the higher you go, and thin, dry air loses its heat fast after sunset, so the plateau vineyards of Coahuila around 1,500 metres and Querétaro near 2,000 metres get the cool nights that keep acid in the grapes. In Baja, the Court's other physical feature, the Pacific does the same work with fog and breezes.

questions.q: Which material does the Court say Mexico's vineyard soils are mixed with in abundance?
questions.exp: The Court describes Mexican soils as mixed with lots of sand, and in the Valle de Guadalupe the slopes are decomposed granite and sand above an alluvial valley floor. Its grape growing cell draws the consequence: sandy soils keep phylloxera away, since the louse does poorly in loose sand, so many vines can grow on their own roots.

questions.q: Which approach does the Court say characterises Mexican winemaking?
questions.exp: With no single signature grape, Mexican winemakers blend freely across Italian, Spanish and French varieties, Nebbiolo or Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache and Merlot, in ways no European appellation would permit; a label may say ensamble for a blend. At the Certified level the Court adds that the aim is premium wine, with some new oak.

questions.q: Beside Chenin Blanc, Viognier and Sauvignon Blanc, which white grape completes the Court's list for Mexico?
questions.exp: Chardonnay is a smaller white in Mexico, made as rich still wine and used as a base for Querétaro's sparkling wine, beside the long-established Chenin Blanc of Baja and Coahuila. The Court's whites run from crisp and dry to round and full according to the grape, Sauvignon Blanc at the crisp end and Viognier at the round.

questions.q: Baja California's emblematic red often surprises a guest who knows the grape only from Barolo. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Nebbiolo has become Baja's emblematic red, but the warm valley makes it darker, softer and riper than Barolo, and DNA work has shown that some vines planted under the name are something else. The Court's red list mixes Spain, Italy and France: Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Zinfandel, Grenache and Barbera.

questions.q: By the Court's figure, what share of Mexico's wine comes from Baja California's Valle de Guadalupe?
questions.exp: The Court credits Baja California and the Valle de Guadalupe, inland from Ensenada, with 90 per cent of Mexican wine; other estimates run somewhat lower, but every count puts the peninsula far ahead. The valley lies some fifty kilometres south of the United States border as the crow flies, at about thirty-two degrees north.

questions.q: Why does the Court say Mexico's fruit-driven, deeply coloured red wines carry elevated alcohol?
questions.exp: Long, sunny, warm growing seasons ripen the grapes to high sugar, which ferments to high alcohol, and the same sun deepens colour and ripens the fruit, so Mexican reds are fruit-driven, deeply coloured and strong. The whites, by the Court's account, run from crisp and dry to round and full-bodied depending on the grape.

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador defeated the Aztec Empire in the 1520s and claimed it for Spain, opening New Spain to the vine?
questions.exp: Hernán Cortés took the Aztec capital in 1521, and an ordinance of 1524, issued in the crown's name, obliged settlers to plant vines in proportion to the native labour they held: the start of what the Court calls the oldest wine industry outside Europe. Casa Madero at Parras, founded in 1597, is the oldest winery still working in the Americas.

questions.q: Spanish law prohibited winemaking in New Spain from 1595. By the Court's account, in which year did Mexican independence end that ban?
questions.exp: In 1595 the Spanish crown barred new vineyards and winemaking in New Spain to protect the wine shipped from Spain, so only missions and a few haciendas kept their vines until independence in 1821 ended the ban. Brandy, not wine, carried most of the twentieth century, and the Court dates the advance of modern Mexican wine from the 1970s.
